CONTRIBUTES TO HEINE MEMORIAL Berlin ( J . T . A . )—Duesseldorf , Heinrich Heines birthplace , where the on of a memorial to the poet prohibited during the regime of Wilhelm II , has conferred recognition upon its distinguished son . The City Council in session voted the first allotment toward the fund necessary for the erection of a Heine memorial in the city . DELEGATED TO COMMANDER BYRDS EXPEDITION Freeport , L . I . ( J . T . A . )—The honor of being the first enlisted man ever chosen to represent the United States army on an exploring expedition has fallen to Staff Sergeant Benjamin Roth of the Sixty-first Aero Squadron of the United States Army Air Service . He has been designated by the War Department to join Commander Byrd s Anarctic Expedition and will leave with the Commander s party on October 1 . Sergeant Roth , who has been in the army fourteen years , is an expert on air-cooled airplane motors . A dinner was given in his honor by tl Freeport Lodge of the Elks , of which he is a member . ANTI-SEMITIC LEADER ARRESTED Warsaw ( J . T . A . )—J . Chamiec , Polish lecturer , one of the notorious anti-Semitic agitators , was arrested at his hotel by the Warsaw police on charges of fraud and blackmail . Hiamiec , a self-styled professor , recently toured the country in the interests of the Polish boycott organization , Rozwoj , preaching everywhere the gospel of hatred and discrimination against Jews . It was now disclosed that during his visit to many towns he obtained large sums of money through blackmailing and extortion methods from Polish merchants . GOVERNMENT TAKES DRASTIC MEASURES Kovno ( J . T . A . )—Three Lithuanian officials in Wolkowishki , Lithuania , where serious anti-Jewish excesses occurred last week , resulting in 20 injured , were dismissed from their posts by an order of the Kovno government .</p><p dir="auto">The officials will soon be tried . The three , the secretary of the County Council , the tax inspector and the detective in charge of the criminal division of the local police , were charged with organizing the anti-Jewish riot . It was said to be the first instance of the Lithuanian government taking drastic measures against those responsible for anti-Jewish disturbances . STUDENTS REFUSED ADMITTANCE Riga ( J . T . A . )—Two hundred and fifty students who applied for admittance to the University of Riga were rejected . The cause of their rejection was said to be their insufficient mastery of the Lettish language , one of the several folk languages in Europe which have gained the status of university discipline since the World War . Ninety Jewish students were admitted to the university . * * * Lemberg , Sept . 22—Three hundred applicants , nearly all Jewish , for admission to the medical school of the University of Lemberg were rejected at the beginning of this semester . Of the 120 students admitted , ten are Jewish . To the law school of the University 541 students were admitted , of whom 126 are Jewish ; in the Department of Natural Sciences 227 students were admitted , of whom 95 were Jews . MARTIAL LAW DECLARED Belgrade ( J . T . A . )—Martial law was declared by the Jugoslav government in Petrovo Selo and the vicinity , the scene of the ritual murder agitation on the eve of Rosh Hashonoh . Rosh Hashonoh passed quietly but in a painful atmosphere for the Jewish community . On Saturday morning , it was discovered that the previous night the Jewish houses in the town were painted with inciting inscriptions . Hotels and public inns in the city were closed and people were prohibited from going abroad in the evening unless they were provided with special permits . The Belgrade government despatched a special ministerial commission to Petrovo Selo with full power to take measures for the maintenance of order and the protection of the Jewish population . WITNESSES AFRAID TO TESTIFY New York ( J . T . A . )—Through intimidation witnesses refused to testify at the trial of ten prisoners charged with complicity in the bombing of the home of Joseph Hasenfratz , in the poultry war which has been going on . Magistrate Reynolds , despite his failure to compel witnesses to give testimony , held over the prisoners . Hasenfratz himself , looking around the courtroom filled with men identified as members of the poultry gang , refused to explain why his home had been bombed . Charles Governan , a witness , refused to testify , saying : I want to have my life and the lives of my family . The prisoners are David Kaufman , David Dickman , David Hirshon , Arthur Herbert , Charles Herbert , Joseph Weiner , Myra Shapiro , Max Keslin , Sidney Rosenstein and Julius Rosenstein . A . )—Senor Paralhos , Brazilian Consul at Bremen , is now in a Bremen hospital where he was taken in an unconscious state because anti-Semitic ringleaders did not know of the adage that appearances are often misleading . It is predicted here that the outrage committed on the Consul will have diplomatic consequences . A . )—The entry and circulation of the Bulletin of the Jewish Telegraphic Agency in any language has been prohibited in Roumainia , according to the Buletinul de Import-Export No . 24 , which published the text of a circular issued by the General Direction of Customs No . 165 , 466 . No reason was given for the prohibition . The circular states : On the ground of a commuication from the Police Direction and the General Sigurantza , on the intervention of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs , we ask you to prohibit the entry and circulation in this country of the Bulletins of the Jewish Telegraphic Agency in any language . You will in consequence take all measures which you consider necessary . The circular is signed by Director Ch . T . Cristea and Chief of Service Vas . C . Vrana . * * * Jacob Landau , managing director of the Jewish Telegraphic Agency , in commenting upon the despatch of the order issued by the Roumanian authorities declared : The order of the Roumanian authorities comes as a complete surprise . The Jewish Telegraphic Agency at all times has been anxious to present the Jewish developments in Roumania accurately and objectively . It has always striven to give both sides of the question and has in every circumstance demonstrated an earnest desire at fair reporting of the facts . The action would be understandable while not excusable if the Roumanian government had further tightened the censorship on Jewish news from Roumania , but the placing of an embargo on Jewish news from all over the world is indeed not only a puzzle , but seems rather a harsh and unjustifiable measure inflicted upon the Jews of Roumania who are thus isolated from the stream of Jewish life everywhere . REV . MARLIN EXPRESSES REGRETS New York ( J . T . A . )—Rev . H . H . Marlin , editorial writer of the United Presbyterian , a religious weekly published in Pittsburgh , who was recently criticized in the Anglo-Jewish press for unfriendly comment made in the United Presbyterian of August 2 , 1928 , in connection with the publication by the Department of Commerce of the results of its census of Jewish religious bodies , indicating the number of the Jewish population , expressed his regrets at the statements he had made . The Rev . Marlin virtually withdrew his statements and gave the assurance that the generalization in which he indulged was a serious mistake which will not be repeated . I am sorry I wrote that editorial , Rev . Marlin wrote . It was written in the spirit of sincerity and without any feeling of animosity to the Jewish race . The United Presbyterian is not unfriendly to your people . Quite the contrary . In the two pages which I have edited for many years in the United Presbyterian I have spoken in the highest terms at various times concerning the great outstanding characters of the Jewish people . The editorial of which you complain is partly complimentary , but there are some statements there which are wounding to the Jewish heart and we very much regret them . I attempted a brief characterization of the Jew as he is generally viewed by Gentile eyes . It is not wise nor just to indulge in that sort of generalization . It was a serious mistake and a mistake which will not be made a second time . I am certainly not an enemy of the Jew . To no other race do I owe so profound a debt as I owe to the Jewish race .</p>

<p dir="auto">National Geographic Society Surveys Palestine</p><p dir="auto">Washington , D . C . —Another survey of Palestine has been made . The facts , old and new , in retrospect and perspective , were again reviewed , recast and presented in relation to the question of the establishment of the Jewish National Home . The National Geographic Society , founded in 1888 for the increase and diffusion of geographic knowledge , with headquarters in Washington , D . C , took a geographic inventory of Palestine as it appears in 1929 and in a release declares that the survey reveals Palestine as a country on the make . Today the Jordan River has been crossed again—by the dam of a power project . Crusaders from Europe once more invade the land , fighting—the mosquitoes who infected 64 per cent of the new settlers with malaria . The land of milk and honey flows—with oranges and Portland cement . Nazareth is a town famous throughout Palestine as the home of , —a new water system . Within the walls of Jerusalem rises a new temple—a $ 2 , 000 , 000 museum of archaeology presented by an American philanthropist . Jehu chauffeurs drive furiously over the hills to Jezreel— -not to wreak vengeance on Jezebel , but to transport some of the 50 , 000 tourists using the Bible as a guidebook . Motor cars on the modern Jezreel road make the chariot speed record of the original Jehu II ( Kings , 9 : 20 ) , patron saint of taxicab drivers , seem a mere snail s pace . Indeed , from Dan , in the north , to Beersheba , in the south , the length of Palestine , is a pleasant day s motor tour . Where Richard the Lion Hearted ruled in Haifa there is a Norman castle—at least it looks like a Norman castle , but it is an electric powerhouse . Progress reaches even to the little town of Bethlehem , where a new hospital is under construction . Even the age-old cry of the Jews has been changed . The wail of 2 , 000 years of yesterdays , Next year in Zion , has become Tomorrow , Zion . Tel Aviv is called the first Hebrew city since the destruction of the temple . There is more to post-war Zionism than Tel Aviv . While this new allJewish community of 40 , 000 is the largest , there are more than 100 other Jewish colonies . Since the Balfour Declaration of 1917 recognized the special interests of Jews in Palestine , the Jewish population has increased from about 70 , 000 in 1920 to more than 150 , 000 . Jews are still a minority in their homeland , however , numbering but one-fifth of the total population . Israel s ten tribes lived off the land . Driven out of Israel into the corners of the world , they made those corner shops and banks . Reconquest of their Palestine homeland once more requires agricultural skill of the Jews . Some of the new settlers , former druggists , clerks , grocers in Russia , studied agriculture two years before coming to Palestine . Good orange , growers will inherit the Holy Land . Yet there is a movement by the Jewish immigrants to make Palestine a glorified department store of the awakening Near East . Already they are selling stockings in Egypt , cement to Syria and Cyprus , perfume to France , oranges to England , and made-in-Palestine unleavened bread all over the world . It is plain that the reconquest of Palestine must come by economic development , not sentiment . The Zionist movement rides two economic horses , pioneering and industry . Pioneers of the American West found free land and lots of it . Jewish pio</p><p dir="auto">neers in Palestine must buy the land and a whole community must live on an acreage equal to a moderate-sized Middle West farm . American pioneers found forests ; the hills of Judea must be re-forested . Americans found a healthy land ; the Jewish settlers fight the mosquito , tropical diseases and a whole catalogue of scourges that attack their orange and almond groves , vineyards and grain fields . From 1919 to 1924 the Zionist movement cost about $ 35 , 000 , 000 and only a few communities have begun to break even , much less pay interest on loans . Industrial conquest relies on a triple program already under way : Haifa Harbor , the Jordan River and the Dead Sea salts . First , the $ 5 , - 000 , 000 Haifa Harbor development will give Palestine its only deep water port . Secondly , the railroad running inland from Haifa to the Jordan River now carries supplies for the hydro-electric development ( the first in Asia Minor , it is declared ) which will turn the 165-foot drop between the Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea into 70 million kilowatt hours per year to light up Palestine . At present there is only a market for 20 million kilowatt hours , but wait and see , say the Zionists . Thirdly , it has been established that the salts of the Dead Sea contain potash in a form usable for the world trade . The chemical extraction problem has been solved . The Jordan development will supply power . Extension of the Haifa Railroad will supply transportation from the 1 , 300-foot sub-sea-level Dead Sea to the new Haifa port , where all except the biggest liners can dock . Jewish capital and brains and British aid move toward the goal . Palestine is not a large country . New Hampshire is slightly larger . Palestine , like New Hampshire , has a mountain range down its middle . New Palestine , nevertheless , deals in millions . Government nurseries now produce more than a million trees annually for reforestation , more than 11 , 000 , 000 telephone calls were made and 12 , 000 , 000 letters were handled in 1927 , more than 2 , 000 , 000 boxes of oranges were shipped out . Foreign trade has increased approximated $ 5 , 000 , 000 since 1924 . Life is complicated by the existence of three official languages . Palestine pounds ( equal to British pounds ) and the subsidiary coins , mils of various denominations , display their values in English , Hebrew and Arabic . They circulate in Palestine , Palestina , or Falastin , depending on your particular faith . The railroad station of the city , sacred to Moslems , Jews and Christians , welcomes them respectively with the words , El Quads esh Sherif , Yerushalayim , and Jerusalem . When archaeologists engaging in one of the country s chief industries , dig up a town , they find remains of each civilization hidden by the one on top . Not so with the human layers that have been spread over this footpath between Asia and Africa . Remnants of races and peoples mill about in the currents of Holy Land life , seldom mixing . The few Samaritans at Nablus are survivors of a colony established bv Sargon II , King of Assyria , 722 B . C . There was a large attendance at the Jewish Social Club on Sunday evening, July 1st, when a welcome was tendered to Miss Vera Ziman upon her return from her visit to Palestine. The function was under the auspices of the Auckland Women’s Zionist Society,'the Auckland Zionist Society and the Auckland Jewish Social Club. Mr N. Alfred Nathan, President of the Auckland Hebrew Congregation, presided. The Chairman said that they all extended to Miss Ziman an enthusiastic welcome on her return from Palestine. They were, however,</p><p dir="auto">represented by Mr and Mrs Nat Madison. IMPRESSIONS OF PALESTINE. Miss Ziman before giving impressions of her tour, thanked the Chairman for his kind words of welcome. The cordial reception she had received in Palestine was due to the fact that she was a Jewess from New Zealand. The women of New Zealand had a warm place in the hearts of their Jewish sisters in Palestine. New Zealand sounded to them like El Dorado. Palestine was a land teeming with tradition. It had made a very deep impression upon her and she loved it very dearly. The Jewish atmosphere absolutely animated the people. They do not say: “I must do for me” but “we must do for us.” Many thousands had settled in Palestine. They were idealists in the best sense of the word. There was something about Palestine that drew them to it. Two days after her stay in Tel-aviv she felt as though she had lived there all her life. With Mrs Caselberg sho had the pleasure of meeting many wonderful people—-with names that were famous among all Jews. After a short description of her stay in Egypt Miss Ziman took her audience with her on a tour of Palestine. It was a thrill to put one’s foot on the soil of Erez Israel, as journeying across the desert they first saw the morning star shining over their own land. THE INFANT WELFARE CENTRE. It was too wonderful to see the New Zealand Infant Welfare Centre in Nordia. It was a link with a dream from Auckland which came true and she wished that the other keen workers of their Society could have been with her and shared her joy. It was good to see the beautiful babies and to hear how thankful the mothers were. They made a confidant of the nurses and doctors, and they expressed openly how thankful they were to their sisters in New Zealand who had worked so hard for them. They were fortunate to have the services of a wonderful doctor, Dr. Zlocisti. Mrs Doniach, the Secretary of the Women’s Zionist Movement to which New Zealand is affiliated, took her down to the New Zealand Infant Welfare Centre on her first visit. The mothers at Nordia were very anxious to learn. The Doctor said he was often the advocate of the baby against the</p><p dir="auto">grandmothers. The Sydney Centre had the same problems. It was in the heart of the Yemenite Centre. The Melbourne Centre was in Ncveh Shalom which was the poorest part of Tel-aviv. The nurses had to speak many languages as Hebrew is not yet entirely spoken by the people. There were all types, Ashkenazi, Caucasian and Sephardic. Miss Ziman naturally spent a great deal of time at Tel-aviv in connection with the Infant Welfare Centres. Some of the most interesting hours she spentS were when together with the different nurses they paid home visits. This was a most important part of the work and it gave her an insight into the types of homes and lives of the people of Tel-aviv. In Nordia, where many of the immigrants settled on arrival and where the New Zealand Centre was situated the homes were mostly barracks. They were kept very clean. The mothers wore of a high standard of intelligence and made the very best use of the help and instruction given by the Doctor and nurses whose patience was wonderful to see. The appreciation shown by the mothers and the welcome afforded the nurses on their visits to the homes of the women attending all the centres was very gratifying. TEL-AVIV. Tel-aviv was an all Hebrew Centre, not only municipally but in literature and language. It was an all Hebrew everything. The people were all Jews trying to make Hebrew the standard language. In the schools even arithmetic is taught in Hebrew. The children all speak it, not only in school but at play and the parents learnt it from their children. Tel-aviv was a modern town which sprung into being in seven years. It now had a population of 35,000. At Tel-aviv she met Mr Louis Kahn, formerly of Auckland, who had settled in Palestine about ten years ago. He has a large orange grove at Petach Tikvah. He was very happy to be there. He sent his greetings to his many friends in Auckland. He said he would like to see a little Auckland community around him in Telaviv. Miss Ziman said that with Mrs Caseb berg she had then made a motor tour through Palestine and she was able to see what a wonderfully beautiful country Palestine was. It was the month of March. Wild flowers were springing up and myriads of insects and birds filled the scented air with music. The</p><p dir="auto">fields were golden with daisies, and even on the Judean hills every bit of earth was covered with scarlet anemones, little blue irises, tulips, wild cyclamen and hundreds of other foliage. The light and colour in Palestine was very vivid. There was no sunshine like Palestine sunshine. TIBERIAS. The historic relics of Palestine were of great interest. There were historic remains from the days of the Romans to the time of Napoleon down to the present day. Our biblical land was full of antiquities. The ruins were a magnificent sight. At Sabashiy, Herod’s temple was still to be seen. The old and the new were a constant contrast. Palestine was now the heart of perhaps the greatest romance of the world, transferred from swamp to fertile country, where there were now groups of little colonies. They had to fight against enormous odds. In New Zealand it had taken us a hundred years to get where we are now. We have forests and a splendid rainfall. In the Emek the low-lying land had to be drained. It was ridden with malaria which was driven away by the planting of gum trees. The eucalyptus was known to the Arabs as the Jew’s tree. The gum tree had served to bring rainfall and in swampy parts large forests have grown to such an extent that when three years old the trees may be cut and the timber used and the stumps then start growing again. From Arfulle there are several colonies quite easy of access—Balfouria, named after Earl Balfour, the children’s village of Kwar Yelladim, where there are children brought from Ukraine, and Ain Charot, a co-operative colony. They then drove to Mt. Tabor, a charming place. The mountain rises above the plains of Estravon to a height of 1000 feet. The view is magnificent, with Syria and Mt. Hermon in the distance. From Mt. Tabor they went through the colony of Sedura to Tiberias where there is an ancient Yeshiva. Tiberias teemed with Jewish interest. The old town is picturesque. In fine weather the colouring on Lake Galilee was a vivid sight, the blue sky with the snow clad mountains in the background, the copper tone of the sea with the setting of the sun were all scenes of beauty. As in all Jewish Palestine the Sabbath t ( liere was a day of rest. From Tiberias they went to Dagania</p><p dir="auto">to the foot of Lake Galilee where the sea joined the Jordon and they saw that river so extolled in history being harnessed by the Butenberg scheme to provide power and irrigation for the whole of Palestine. Near Tiberias was the little colony of Migdal which was situated # on the side of Lake Tiberias, a background of high hills. Here they are founding the banana industry of Palestine. Near the town were many tombs of the Prophets, and also of Rabbi Akiba. A new suburb to be named after Sir Herbert Samuel is being built here. They then went North past the Huli sea to Metulla and then to the source of the Jordon. CAPTAIN TRUMPELDOR. Coming back from Metulla they visited Ain Hai, the scene of the tragedy of Captain Trumpeldor. He was the only Jew in the Busso-Japanese war to serve as an officer. He fought at Gallipoli and also with the British in Palestine. He was one of the heroes of Palestine. During an attack on the colony of Ain Hai by Arabs, while defending the colony he fell mortally wounded, and as he died he said: "It is good to die for our country.” The boy scouts in Palestine are called Trumpeldor scouts. During Sir Alfred Mond’s recent visit to Palestine he arranged for the erection of a monument to Trumpeldor on the spot where he fell. Safed, Nazareth and Nahalal followed. Nahalal is to Canada what Infant Welfare is to New Zealand. There they trined girls as agriculturists. Everything was modern and up-to-date. HAIFA. Haifa on the shores of the Mediterranean was a place of great beauty. They are starting to build the new harbour and this will open up great tracts of country. Mt. Carmel overlooks the Haifa Bay to the town of Acre which is full of historic interest and has associations with Napoleon, and more recently with Jabotinsky. The drive back from Acre was very beautiful as the sun set, turning the waves to gold. May it be a symbol that Haifa will bring much gold to Palestine. In Haifa there was a remarkable High School for technical education. All the . subjects were taught through the medium of Hebrew. JERUSALEM. Jerusalem must be seen in the light of its Biblical associations. It brought the past to life. It contained so much</p><p dir="auto">for all Jews. To her the outstanding sight was the Wailing Wall. She was much impressed with the strong religious atmosphere. Jerusalem streets were very narrow and the people were of all kinds and descriptions, speaking many languages. Mt. Scopus and the Hebrew university commanded a view across to the Hills of Moab on one side down to the Mediterranean on the other. The agricultural museums of the Zionist Organisation were of special interest. Professor Warburg, the Head of the Station, was a great lover of Palestine. The Tomb of the Kings and the tomb of Bachel on the road to Bethleham were all visited in turn. The old walls of Jerusalem have been kept repaired all the time. There was a thrill about the sounds of Damascus Gate, Jaffe Gate, the Tower of David and the Golden Gate.</p><p dir="auto">In her concluding remarks Miss Ziman said that the proudest day of their lives was when Mrs Caselberg and she laid the foundation stone of the new building of the New Zealand Infant Welfare Centre. That building will make the name both of New Zealand and of Mr and Mrs David Nathan. In Palestine these names were synonymous. She hoped that xuany of her audience would share theix* great joy and would have the pleasure of seeing the wonderful sights in Palestine. At the conclusion of Miss Ziman’s address, which was beautifully delivered, she was heartily congratulated. It was notable for the vivid description of what Mrs Caselberg and Miss Ziman had seen during their tour. It was permeated by enthusiasm and an ardent Zionist spirit. "Zionism is going to succeed” was the keynote of her remarks, and the audience, as they followed her experiences with rapt attention, all shared her conviction. Miss Ziman in replying, expressed her deep appreciation of the honour paid to her and her parents who had so encouraged her in her work. Bev. S. A. Goldstein, President of the Auckland Zionist Society, joined in the welcome to Miss Ziman. Her address was a great treat. Zionism stood for the spirit of Jewish consciousness. It had given Judaism a new life. In presenting a Golden Book Certificate to Mr Max Bobinson, Hon. Secretary of the Auckland Zionist Society and Joint Hon. Secretary of Dr. A. Goldstein Appeal, Bev. Goldstein said that his enthusiasm for Zionism was unbounded. Zionist work had been to him a pleasure and a delight. Auckland had gained world wide prestige as a greafr Zionist community and they could feel</p><p dir="auto">proud that their Zionist work had ■earned the appreciation of Jewry Overs;as and had given Auckland so high a reputation. Alfred Nathan, who was Chairman of the Dr. Goldstein Committee, the President who had been a tower of strength to the Movement, and in Mrs David Nathan, President of the Women’s Zionist Society, one who was never happier than when she was working for Zionism and Palestine. He also desired to express his appreciation of the cordial goodwill that their nonJewish fellow citizens had always displayed towards the Movement. Zionism was the greatest of all Jewish causes and they felt that by supporting they were furthering the great ideal which reached to the very depths of the Jewish hearts and also commended itself to the greatest minds of their time. He also desired to thank Mr Meltzer and his office staff for valuable assistance rendered on many occasions in connection with Zionist work. Last but not least, he wished to mention the name of New Zealand’s greatest Zionist thinker and worker, Mr Louis Phillips. It was through him that Zionism was such a huge success in Auckland and that Dr. Alexander Goldstein’s visit proved such a triumph. He trusted that he would at all times be worthy of the confidence which they had shown in him by the presentation of ■so beautiful a certificate. MR. MELTZER’S REPLY. Mr I. Meltzer said that he hardly knew how to express adequately his gratitude and appreciation of the fine gift of a Golden Book certificate. He •esteemed it a great honour to have his name, inscribed amongst such names as those Mrs Nathan had just mentioned. Whatever ho might have done for the -cause of Zionism in Auckland was done without any hope of reward. In university and sanctuary it may recreate a spiritual renaissance, a light that will shed luster on the Jewish name to the ends of the earth.</p><p dir="auto">In this article Rabbi Witt, "whose brilliant and forceful keynote lecture at the recent convention of the Union of American Hebrew Congregations in this city will be long remembered, writes tersely and eloquently about the things he saw and felt during his visit to Palestine some years ago.— Editor.</p>

<p dir="auto">OLDNEWLAND</p><p dir="auto">UY THEODOR HERZL</p><p dir="auto">Translated and Abridged by LOTTA LEVEN SOHN</p><p dir="auto">II Haifa, the Port of Palestine Summary of Previous Instalment Friedrich Loewenberg, a young Viennese doctor of law, disheartened by the anti-Semitic obstacles to a career, consents to go to a solitary South Sea island as companion to a Mr. Kingscourt, an elderly, misanthropic (so he claims) German-American millionaire. Before they leave, Kingscourt violates his principles by letting Loewenberg have some money to rehabilitate a Galician peddler’s family named Littwak. In December, 1902, their yacht puts in at Jaffa for a few days thanks to Kingscourt’s lively interest in the "old land of the Jews.” Coming back twenty years later for a peep at the great world, they again stop off at Palestine, and for the same reason. IN the spring of 1923, a little more than twenty years after Kingscourt sank Time into the waters of the Red Sea, his yacht reappeared there, this time heading toward Europe. The charming old hater of his kind was wondering out loud why there was not a sign of all the passenger ships that used to pass through the Red Sea on their way to India, Australia, China, and Japan. Freighters bound for Madagascar and African ports there were aplenty, but no other craft. “Why don’t you ask the pilot?” queried his companion, Dr. Loewenberg, who had spent the intervening years with him on the South Sea island to which they retired in order to escape from humanity. “I’ll ask nothing. I’ll wait till we get to Europe. I’m not curious. Are you, Fritzchen, eh?” “No, Kingscourt. It’s all one to me.” The old man puffed at a thick Havana. “Well, Fritz, our island did not disagree with you. What a green, hollow-chested Jewboy you were when I took you away. Now you are like an oak. You might still be dangerous to the women.” “You’re quite mad, Kingscourt. Are you dragging me to Europe to marry me off?” Kingscourt roared. “What should I do with you then?” “Well, it might be a delicate way of getting rid of me.” “Now he’s fishing for compliments. I arranged this whole trip so you’d be patient with me a few years longer.” “I say, Kingscourt. That’s ...”</p><p dir="auto">“Idiotic?” “Something of the sort. When was I ever impatient? I was very happy on our island. Old man, you ought to be ashamed to offer such rotten pretexts. You’re curious about things over there —not I.” The old man smirked gleefully. “Well, I’ll confess. Yes, I should like to know what has become of the vile world. I do want to see whether the human race is still so stupid and base.” The yacht speeded through the Suez Canal, and they disembarked at Port Said to make some purchases. The port was practically deserted. What had become of the throngs of globe-trotters? They learned from the captain of a German trading vessel that traffic via Europe and Asia had taken a new route, over Palestine. “Are there harbors and railways in Palestine?” asked Loewenberg. “Are there harbors and railways in Palestine! Where do you come from, sir?” “Listen to me, captain,” cried Kingscourt. “We’d like to offer you some good wine. . . . We’re a pair of damned ignorant wretches. Now, then, what’s happened in that old Palestine?” “You could get there in less time than it would take me to tell you about it. Why not make a slight detour if you’ve a few days to spare? If you care to leave your yacht, you’ll find fast boats at Haifa and Jaffa to all the European and American ports." “No, we don’t leave our yacht. But we could make the detour, Fritze. What do you say? Do you want to take another peep at the land of your blessed ancestors?” Loewenberg, the Jew, replied that Palestine attracted him as little as Europe. “It’s all the same to me.” The yacht headed northward for Haifa, and entered its harbor on a lovely, mild spring morning. Kingscourt and Loewenberg stood on the bridge together staring through their telescopes, imagining there must be some mistake. “I could swear that that was the Bay of Acco over there,” remarked Loewenberg. “And I could also swear to the contrary,” asserted Kingscourt. “I remember that Bay very wqll. It was empty and forsaken. However, there’s Mount Carmel</p><p dir="auto">on our right, and over there to the left is the town of Acco.” The skyline of Acco was little changed. It showed the same grey fortress walls, the same heavy cupolas and slender minarets silhouetted against the morning sky. But Haifa was unrecognizable. All the way from Acco to the top of the Carmel it was one great stretch of garden city. Wherever one looked beautiful villas were set in luxuriantly blossoming gardens. And the harbor,* with its great stone dams, had obviously become the safest and most convenient shelter for ships in the whole of the eastern Mediterranean. A whole fleet of ships lay at anchor in the roadstead, flying the flags of every nation. ... It was clear that the world had not stood still during those twenty years. The two friends left the yacht, and were rowed in a landing boat through the swarming ships to the stone quay. As they were walking up the steps to street level,</p><p dir="auto">a young man on his way down to an electric launch that was awaiting him, stopped abruptly to stare at Loewenberg. “Sir!” stormed the hot-headed old Kingscourt, “what do you want of us?” The young man, however, turned to Loewenberg, and addressed him by name in a pleasant voice that trembled somewhat under stress of emotion. “Yes, I am Dr. Friedrich Loewenberg,” replied the person addressed, not concealing his surprise. The stranger fell upon his neck and embraced him impetuously. “And who are you, sir?” asked Loewenberg, as soon as he had recovered his breath.</p><p dir="auto">The tall, sunburnt man of thirty, whose face was framed in a short black beard, replied: “I? Oh, you won’t remember me. My name is David Littwak.” “Not the little fellow from the Cafe Birkenreis?” “Yes, sir. He whom you saved from starvation, with his parents and his sister.” “Please don’t mention it!” “On the contrary, it shall be mentioned a great deal. Whatever I am and whatever I have I owe entirely to you. Now you are my guest. And this gentleman, too, if he is a friend of yours.” “This is the best and only friend I have in the world, Mr. Kingscourt!” rYAVID LITTWAK led his guests up to a great square called the “Place of the Nations.” It was surrounded by handsome buildings in which were housed</p><p dir="auto">the offices of colonial banks and branches of European shipping companies, and crowded with a cosmopolitan throng, which included many Chinese, Persians, and Arabs; but the dominating note was European. It would have been easy to imagine oneself in some Italian port. The sky and sea were brilliantly blue as on the Riviera. But there was very little noise. One heard no hoofbeat of horses, no cracking of whips, no rumbling of wheels. Automobiles speeded by on rubber tires with only an occasional toot of warning. Above the palm trees that lined the square ran an overhead electric train with wheels on the roof gliding along a thick double iron rail. Littwak explained that this was no new invention. Such electric overhead trains were running between Barmen and Elberfeld in the 1890’s. “We installed them as soon as we rebuilt our cities,” said Littwak. “They make street traffic safer</p><p dir="auto">and easier. And they are cheaper to build than elevated or street railways.” * "I beg your pardon!” cried Kingscourt. “You speak of cities! Are there more cities like this in Palestine?” “Don’t you know that, gentlemen?” “Neither that nor anything else,” Loewenberg assured him. “We have been dead for twenty years.” “Indeed, dear Dr. Loewenberg, we thought you dead.” “Did you inquire about me? And how do you happen to know my name? I don’t remember telling it to you at the time.” “We felt very badly when you withdrew from our thanks. Thinking you might be a regular patron of the Cafe Birkenreis, I waited for you many nights in the doorway. My father, too.” “Is your father still alive?” “Yes, thank Heaven, and my mother, too. And Miriam, whom you saw as a baby. . . . Finally, I thought of asking the waiter about you. He recognized my description, but imagine my grief when he told me that the newspapers had reported your death in a mountain accident. We mourned much for you, I can tell you. And we have always lighted the Jahrzeit lamp on the date I found in the papers. . . . But we mustn’t stand here. You are coming with me to Friedrichsheim.” “To ?” “To Friedrichsheim, my home. You will guess in whose honor it was named. We shall drive up.” For all his cordiality, the young man’s tone was firm. “He takes over the command, Fritze,” murmured Kingscourt, not inappreciatively. Some chance remark of David’s caused Kingscourt to ask whether the Return of the Jews to Palestine had actually taken place. “It certainly has.” “Thunder and glory!” shouted Kingscourt. “So they spewed you out of Europe, eh?” “Well, you must not imagine that there was a medieval expulsion. It did not take that form. Not, at least, in the more progressive countries. On the whole, the operation was bloodless. At the turn of the century, life had become intolerable for the Jews. The persecutions were both social and economic. Jewish merchants were boycotted, Jewish workingmen starved out, Jewish professional men proscribed, not to mention the subtle moral sufferings to which a sensitive Jew was exposed. The blood myth was revived. At the same time, Jews were accused of poisoning the press as in the Middle Ages they had been accused of poisoning the wells. Whether Jews were rich or poor or middle-class, they were hated just the same. They were criticized when they enriched themselves, and criticized when they spent their money. They were neither to produce nor to consume. They were forced out of government posts. The law cohirts were prejudiced against them. In such circumstances, they had either to become the deadly enemies of a society so unjust to them,f or seek themselves a refuge from persecution. The latter alternative was adopted. And here we are. We have saved ourselves!” “Old-New-Land!” murmured Loewenberg.</p><p dir="auto">“Indeed,” assented David earnestly, “it is just that. We have set up a New Society on our old soil.” “The Devil!” shouted Kingscourt. “All that’s frightfully interesting. There’s a tremendous lot to see here. . . .” “I shall show you everything.” “Listen to me, esteemed man and Jew. I must anticipate with a confession. Otherwise, you may repent your attentions to me. lam not a Jew. Now that you know, will you throw me out, or just disgorge me gently?” “Oh, I say, Kingscourt!” deprecated Loewenberg. “I had already guessed that you were not a Jew," replied David calmly. “Let me tell you, then, that my associates and I make no distinctions between one man and another. We do not ask to what race or religion a man belongs. If he is a man, that suffices us.” “Bombs and howitzers! And do all the inhabitants of this region think so?” “I did not say that,” admitted David. “There are other views among us as well.” “Aha! I thought so at once, esteemed lover of mankind.” “I shall not bore you now with our political controversies. But the fundamental principles of humanitarianism are generally respected among us. As for religious tolerance, you will find Christian, Mohammedan, Buddhist and Brahmin houses of worship near our own synagogues.” A S they drove through the city, the travellers glimpsed a fascinating variety of architectural styles. The dwelling houses were small and charming like those of the Belgian cities, and were usually intended for only one family. The great public and commercial buildings were all the more imposing by contrast. Littwak named several as they passed: the Marine Department, the Department of Commerce, the Employment Department, the Department of Education, the Department of Electricity, the Building Department—the latter a particularly handsome structure with a frescoed loggia. This was the headquarters of Steineck, the chief architect of Old-New-Land, who had made the plans for the cities. “That man had a large task,” observed Loewenberg. “But a very grateful one. Like the rest of us, he had abundant materials from which to create. Nbver in history have cities been built so quickly or so well, because never before have so many technical facilities been available. We merely had to transplant existing devices.” By this time they had reached a residential suburb on the top of Mount Carmel,* where they saw many beautiful homes and gardens. In front of a house of Moorish design with close wooden lattices on some of its windows stood a handsome man of about thirty-five. “There’s my friend Reschid Bey," said David. Reschid, who was wearing dark European clothing and a red fez, saluted them with the Oriental gesture that signifies picking up the dust and kissing it. David called to him in Arabic, and Reschid replied in German. Kingscourt stared. “Who’s the little Mussulman?” “He studied in Berlin,” replied David laughingly. “His father was among the first to understand the beneficent character of the Jewish immigration, and so enriched</p><p dir="auto">himself. Reschid himself is a member of our New Society.” “What New Society?” asked Loewenberg. “Dearly beloved,” added Kingscourt, “you must instruct us, like newborn calves, in all that’s worth knowing. We know neither the old nor the new society.” “All shall be explained to you in due course.” The serpentine road from the town to the top of the mountain opened wide prospects of the city and harbor of Haifa, of the broad Bay of Acco with its zone of gardens,* the town of Acco with its background of mountains. The Mediterranean glittered blue and gold into an infinite horizon, and white-capped waves fluttered toward the brown strand. As they alighted near the summit to get a better view of the landscape, David faced about, saying, “See, Dr. Loewenberg, this is the land of our fathers!” Loewenberg was touched to the quick by these words. He recalled the moonlit Death that had been Jerusalem twenty years before; here was Palestine come alive, sparkling joyously in the sun. And this free, vigorous, educated man who gazed at one so steadfastly and seemed to stand so firmly in his shoes was the erstwhile Jewish beggar boy. It appeared that he was a prominent citizen, too. Many people had bowed to him on the drive through the city. For a moment Loewenberg thought he could discern in this upstanding David Littwak some trace of the boy in the Viennese slum who had doggedly announced that one day he would return to the Land of Israel. U'RIEDRICHSHEIM was a large, handsome villa r with extensive grounds. A stone lion crouching before the entrance to the house reminded Loewenberg how the peddler’s boy had cried out: “The lion Judah once had, he can have again! Our old God still lives!” And the dream had been fulfilled. Littwak’s wife and sister welcomed Loewenberg happily, as though he were an old friend. Before showing him and Kingscourt to their rooms, however, David took them to the nursery, where they found his baby son Friedrich (named, of course, in honor of Loewenberg’s “memory”) enthroned in a high chair. The child was at once fascinated by Kingscourt’s long white beard and held out his little arms to the old man, who was flattered and captivated by the attention. And from that moment the Prussian ex-cavalry officer became the bounden slave of the youngest Littwak, who ruled over him with a tyrannical hand. A delicious luncheon was served in the panelled dining room. Kingscourt complimented his host on the wines. They were all Palestinian, he was told, some of them from David’s own vineyards. The first Jewish villages had, in fact, begun with viniculture in the 1880’s, when the best varieties of foreign vines had been imported and had thriven well. Miriam excused herself before the end of the meal. After she had left the room, David explained that she taught French and English at a girls’ high schoo.l. His sister did not have to teach for a livelihood (this in reply to Kingscourt’s growl that it was “too bad the poor girl had to drudge at giving lessons!”); but she was a mem-</p><p dir="auto">ber of the New Society with equal rights. She therefore had corresponding duties to perform. “All the Devils!” exclaimed Kingscourt, with the surprise natural to a gentleman whose notions of women’s rights dated back to 1902. “Yes,” repeated David, “they have both active and passive suffrage here. During the reconstruction period, their enthusiasm lent wings to the men’s courage. We could not decently have relegated them to the servants’ hall or the harem when all was completed. “Our women are not, of course, compelled to exercise their rights, nor do they do so to the point where the well-being of their families would be jeopardized. They are too sensible for that. Besides, it is a common human trait, and not merely a feminine one, that we do not concern ourselves too much with rights we have already won. . . . “The way for equal rights for women had been paved in other countries. Women had long had the suffrage in local representative bodies and professional organizations. They were found to waste no more time than the men, and to talk no more foolishly. In fact, they showed much ability and cleverness. Why should we have let all that valuable experience go to waste?”* “For the rest,” he continued, “politics is neither a business nor a profession in Old-New-Land. Our courts have repeatedly ruled in slander suitsi that the term ‘professional politicians,’ is of opprobrious intent.” “But, how, in that case,” inquired Loewenberg, “do you fill your public offices?” “There are both salaried and honorary positions. The salaried positions are allotted on the basis of skill and merit only. We do not permit our paid officials to participate in public discussion. The status of the honorary officials is very different. We ignore men who push themselves forward for such posts, and do our best to seek out real ability, even in the most obscure corners.” In reply to further questions put by his guests at the luncheon table, David went on to tell them how, in Old-New-Land, all types of benevolent and social welfare institutions, such as hospitals, infirmaries, public kitchens, vacation camps, and so on, had been merged into a single administrative unit, so that every sick or needy applicant could be cared for. Yes, there were poor even here, because it had not been possible to change human nature. People were still brought low by their own vices, or by misfortune, deserved and undeserved. ... No new devices in philanthropy had been invented in Palestine. The old forms and institutions had merely been systematized. It never happened, for instance, that a patient was turned away from hospitals without receiving medical aid. By a little forethought, matters had been so arranged that a bed was always promptly available in one hospital or another. The same thing with employment. Work was found by the public employment exchanges for all who applied, beggary was not tolerated. Healthy persons caught begging were sentenced to hard labor. “All that must be very expensive,” said Loewenberg.
