<p dir="auto">FROM TOWN AND COUNTRY</p><p dir="auto">THE GENESIS OF CREATION Pardess Anna | N the beginning the area which is now Pardess Anna* and</p><p dir="auto">environs was without form and void, but the earth of itself brought forth wild grass and flower and tree and was good to look at. Someone saw visions of fruitful existence in spite of the sand dunes around, and the land was bought from a family which some eighty years ago were Moslem refugees from Bosnia. The head of the family was made an official under the Turkish regime, and the land, given to him by a benevolent Sultan, had remained uncultivated until it was sold to the Palestine Jewish Colonisation Association- (P.I.C.A.). Plans were then drawn and calculations made of so many dunams, so many orange trees, so much labour, so many men, so many families, and so much money. Swamps were drained, water was found, reservoirs were built, roads were planned, the lay-out of a settlement sketched, and settlement began.</p><p dir="auto">First there came three young men, a German, a Russian and an Englishman, the third educated as a farmer; all three had worked as agriculturalists for a number of years in various parts of Palestine, and so had met and become friends. When they heard of a new area to be opened up, they combined their interests, and in 1927 bought between them from the P.I.C.A. an area of some 300 dunams which they called Tel Alon—the hill of oaks, because of the many such trees that grew all around. These were old trees of goodly size and appearance although on approach one saw a huge hollow scooped out in most of the trunks which had been used as a fireplace for cooking by wandering Beduin. Time was when forests of oak stretched all over the locality but the last world War saw the remnants of these forests cut down by the Turks to serve as fuel for the railway service.</p><p dir="auto">Each of the three young men had means to develop his property : they bored for and found water, they built a two-storey house for their own accommodation, and another for their workmen in addition to stable and stores, and they planted orange groves in the sandy waste. Their house was conspicuous from the distance and passing travellers were prone to visit them from curiosity and interest, and always found food to eat and a bed to sleep in as occasion demanded. Other people bought land from the P.I.C.A. and bored for water and planted orange groves, some for themselves, but most as investments for people living abroad who intended to come when their groves would bring in the means whereby they could live. Thus a second area was called Meged. Now others came to work in this almost uninhabited neighbourhood and in 1932 a business organisation built cottages and stables on a number of small allotments on the land belonging to the P.I.C.A. and sold them to the workers on a longterm instalment plan. This was the beginning of the workers suburb of Tel Zvi, which is near Tel Alon and Meged: many orange trees were planted on these holdings by the workers.</p><p dir="auto">Pardess Anna itself came gradually into being from the year 1929 when some ten men, who lived in temporary huts and tents and ate in an improvised wooden canteen, came to work for the P.I.C.A. Cottages were built for them on a hill which was all sand and which overlooked an expanse of dunes stretching from the eucalyptus woods bordering Hadera to the Mediterranean Sea : their families joined them, they were supplied with a small stock of cattle and poultry, all on the same long-term instalment plan, and they gradually planted their holdings with citrus in addition to the regular vegetable and fruit garden. The P.I.C.A. planted a large citrus nursery as the foundation of their programme of settlement for Pardess Anna, and when in 1929 the first group of settlers came, their work on this nursery helped them to augment their limited budget. The plan provided for each settler an area of 20 dunams for pardess (orchard) and</p><p dir="auto">5 dunams for house and farm, and in addition 10 dunams for afforestation: they built ten cottages, similar to those in the workers quarters, for the first settlers who were all young men —most of them newly married —the majority of whom had received an agricultural training in Germany, France or Palestine, and had worked as agricultural labourers in Palestine. The capital investment demanded from them was £500, which was estimated to cover their living expenses and the cost of developing their orchards with the help of supplementary earnings as labourers, for a period of five years, when their groves were to come in bearing. The cost of land, water installation, and cottage, was charged as a long-term loan payable with the development of their orange groves. This development was calculated on so many trees to a dunam, so many cases of fruit to a tree, so many shillings to a case, the number of shillings being limited but steady, while the number of cases were to rise year by year until the debts for land and buildings were paid during a period of 18 years, and the orange grower gradually relaxed from his strenuous labour. Almost together with the first group, came a second type of settler who possessed a capital of £800, thus being able to build his own more comfortable house at an approximate cost of £300 as compared with the P.I.C.A. cottage which had cost some £160. The difference in cost meant more convenient sanitary arrangements, a real bathroom instead of an elementary shower, and in some cases three rooms instead of two. In return for this larger capital investment, he was privileged to choose his own pardess and building site, while the smaller capitalist had to take his chance by drawing lots: and to this day we have our Five Hundred Street and our Eight Hundred Street, although there are several smaller cottages on the latter street and a couple of handsome houses, which cost considerably more than £300 plus £160 on the first street: but of these, more anon. In the course of the period from 1927 to 1934, when the onfall of German settlers reached its height, there was a gradual growth of settlement and orange plantation, and a permanent population, including workers and their families, of some one thousand souls now live here, while large tracts of country around have been transformed into groves of trees swaying in the wind, and bright in the sunlight. El Kay A PORT FOR TEL AVIV Tel Aviv, June 8, 1936. "J" HE prestige of Tel Aviv has never stood as high as it does today. As the military convoy leaves the Jerusalem bus caravan in Herzl Street, one escapes from the shadow of its machine gun into an atmosphere different from curfew-ridden Jerusalem. Gone is that supercilious attitude towards precocious Tel Aviv, now come of age in more than one sense. In Tel Aviv life flows normally, but not merely have its citizens succeeded in carrying on despite the terrorism outside; they have also succeeded in remaining unflurried and unprovoked. This is a young town : not only because its population is composed of so many youths—the adults and the middle-aged are young, too. And youth is usually impetuous and often irresponsible. So the unruffled and unexacerbated town of 150,000 inhabitants has earned admiration for its dignity and humanity, as well as for the many other attributes which make up this wonder city. The Tel Avivians are not unmindful of their new conquest. They never accepted the inferior status to which the capital was wont to relegate them, but now that Jerusalem is actually jealous of their security, their freedom, their savoir-faire, they indulge in some self-satisfaction. But not complacency—enthusiasm still pumps fresh vitality into their plans. Now, of course, the focus of energy is the future port. Will there be a port at Tel Aviv ? To ask the question is almost like heresy. But I found that while the population is determined never to go back to the old conditions of the Jaffa Port, which is hardly more</p><p dir="auto">of a safe anchorage than the shore of Tel Aviv, they are not blinded by any illusions in regard to the practical side of the question. The LP.100,000 which has almost all been subscribed, is estimated to cover the cost of a break-water and a concrete jetty. With the widening of the mouth of the Auja, these works would make loading and off-loading as safe as in Jaffa today. But will the Government, which has invested so many hundreds of thousands of pounds in improving the wharf at Jaffa, erected custom and storage sheds and port offices there, give up Jaffa, or permit a duplicate port construction a few kilometres distant ? There is no doubt in the mind of Tel Aviv that Haifa harbour cannot hope adequately to cope with the future trade of Palestine. That has been conceded also by the Government experts. Tel Aviv and its Jewish hinterland even now can keep a modest port busy and when we add the large trade of Jewish Jerusalem, the proposition becomes very real. I understand that a Tel Aviv Port has been supported by Mr. Shelley, the British Chairman of the Jerusalem Chamber of Commerce. Tel Aviv did not always insist upon separating its maritime activity from Jaffa. It is too hard-headed. The proposal which Mr. Dizengoff, its Mayor, kept repeating to the Government here and in London, was for a greater Jaffa-Tel Aviv harbour, mid-way between the two towns, to be constructed in such a fashion that if and when desired, goods could be loaded or off-loaded on the Tel Aviv shore. The situation hitherto, in which Tel Aviv goods have had to be taken off at Jaffa, and at tremendous expense hauled around the town and over a steep hill, before they could reach their destination, was economically quite unjustifiable. When in addition conditions arise as at present, and it is positively unsafe for Jews to be found in Jaffa, it is clear that an end must be put to such conditions. It costs as much, I believe, to bring heavy merchandise from Jaffa Port to Tel Aviv, as from Jerusalem to Tel Aviv.</p><p dir="auto">At one time a proposal was made to build a harbour at Jaffa, and to construct a coastal road to it from Tel Aviv, so that consignees from the latter town would not have to go through Jaffa. Tel Aviv was even prepared to defray part of the cost of this road, which would have left the port entirely in Jaffa. To-day this scheme has no support whatsoever here. Either there will be a Jaffa —Tel Aviv joint port by constructing a break-water and the necessary facilities near the boundary of the areas of the two municipalities, or there must be port facilities for Tel Aviv itself. If neither of these solutions is adopted, Tel Aviv will import and export through Haifa. That it can maintain its decision not to go back to old Jaffa may be assumed from its attitude to the slaughter-house question. As in the case of so many other public services, slaughtering of cattle for Tel Aviv used to take place only in Jaffa. Government refused permission for Tel Aviv to build its own abattoir. Tel Aviv refrained from eating meat for a month, then obtained its meat from the Jewish villages, and finally Government recognised the right of the larger of the two towns to have its own slaughterhouse. People are saying that similar action may be necessary in order to obtain recognition of Tel Aviv's maturity in the matter of the port. * * * The absorptive capacity of Tel Aviv is already great enough to stand considerable strain. There were 12,000 Jews in Jaffa and most of them have been evacuated into the Jewish town. The organisation of their relief has proceeded almost like a normal function of the Municipal Administration, but Tel Aviv is itching to solve the problem on an enduring basis. It is clear that at least 5,000 of the refugees will never go back to Jaffa —their homes are destroyed and no future awaits them there. They are people mostly of a very modest standard of living. They need to be housed in cottages. Once with a roof over their heads, they will resume their occupations, maintaining themselves and providing work for others. They are largely Jews from Yemen, Iraq and other Eastern countries. I even</p><p dir="auto">saw a refugee, in the double sense, from Abyssinia—a Jewish woman of British nationality who left Jibuti five months ago. On June 17th, Government will cease to contribute 20 mils per day per refugee, half of the cost of living. Then the whole burden will fall upon the Jews themselves, although the refugees from the mixed quarters are not permitted, if they wished, to return there. Neither will the Municipality be permitted to allocate funds for their maintenance. The burden is being placed by Government upon the Jews, here and abroad, whose voluntary contributions are now being collected for the rehabilitation of the victims of disorder. * * * The Levant Fair closed down last night amid scenes of mass enthusiasm. Of course, its success has been greatly reduced by the deterioration of economic conditions owing to public insecurity, but the foreign exhibitors are satisfied to have been here, made connections, and made their products known, so that when conditions are again normal, they may reap the benefit. The usual visitors from Egypt, Syria and Iraq were absent, and even in Palestine the visitors from outside Tel Aviv were much fewer. The depleted revenue from the Fair itself may partly be compensated in another form. It appears that Jewish factories in the neighbourhood of Jaffa wish to transfer to Tel Aviv and pending the erection of their permanent buildings, will use the large pavilions of the exhibition. The Maspero Cigarette factory, which at one time found its Jaffa factory menaced in an ugly situation from which the employees were saved only by prompt police action, is expanding its own exhibit of machinery at the Fair, and will start production in the Palestine Pavilion itself. * * * One of the curious anomalies of this town is its voluntary fire brigade. When it was no more than a little suburb, it was naturally proud of its volunteers who were not indeed often called upon. But it is rather ridiculous for a town of this size to have to depend upon amateurs when a big blaze threatens destruction. The other week volunteers were engaged, together with the Jaffa Fire Brigade, in fighting a timber yard fire in the middle of the night, but their combined efforts failed to save the property. In this country fire brigades appear to be treated by the authorities as a mild luxury. Neither Jerusalem nor Haifa is properly equipped in this respect. There are so many insurance companies in Palestine that they themselves might consider it worth while to defray the cost of professional brigades. * * * The stadium which adjoins the Fair grounds was loaned to the exhibition authorities, but there is much dissatisfaction at its conversion into an Amusement Park. Sportsmen deplore the damage done to the course and the athletic young men are wondering when they will be able to make use of their erstwhile sports ground. So much time can be spent out of doors in Tel Aviv, and so desirable from all points of view is the development of manly exercise and the team spirit which is associated with clean sport, that the stadium should rapidly be restored to its original function. It is no longer far from the city, for a cheap bus ride brings you to it from the centre of the town. Here is an opportunity for friends of Tel Aviv to make this amenity worthy of its youth who during these days of trial have shown such remarkable selfcontrol. E. Zacutta PROGRESS ON THE CARMEL Haifa. Hadar Hacarmel, originally a handful of straggling houses on a ridge half-way up the mountain, at the end of September 1935, had a population of 23,000 souls, representing an increase of 7,000 in a single year. I am told that a further 2,000 persons can now be added to that number, which signifies about 25% of the whole population of Haifa and is indeed a considerable figure anywhere for an area mainly residential. Large-scale business is confined to the town below because of proximity to</p><p dir="auto">the Port, and industry having its own zone on the Haifa Bay. The attraction of the suburb, as very often happens in Jewish settlement, lay and lies in the facilities for education comprised by the schools, the kindergartens, the Technical Institute and the Extension Courses which have blossomed of late into a "Popular University." In the same way Haifa people will tell you that the development of Mount Carmel awaits the opening of the school which is shortly to be built near Ahuzat Sir Herbert Samuel. Haifa has been long notorious for the poor quality of its water, but while a general water supply scheme for the whole town is still on paper, Hadar Hacarmel already receives a far purer liquid from the seepage holes and wells of Emek Zebulun (Haifa Bay), and we are promised that this system, instead of providing water only to the extent of 62 per cent, as last year, the balance being drawn from wells within Hadar, will furnish enough for the whole district in 1936. This supply will also serve some other parts of the town, including Neve Shaanan and Mount Carmel, forming a nucleus for the eventual Haifa Water Supply. The Committee of Hadar Hacarmel has already invested £P. 30,0000 in this enterprise.</p><p dir="auto">A new section has suddenly sprung up in Geula but it suffers from an old parcellation ; (eleven years old, to be accurate, but in Palestine that is already old-fashioned). Overcrowding in this new corner will be avoided by the public park that has been projected near the site for the offices of the"Magen David Adorn." Some weeks ago the Municipal Engineer of Haifa alluded to the relative merits of stone and concrete, and advised giving the former material a chance. It is true that, although blocks of flats are the sole solution for the housing of a growing population, they need not have too markedly the exterior of "tenements." A slight improvement might be afforded by stucco work on prolonged smooth surfaces. Another amelioration would be the more general screening-off of balconies, for even the most lenient-minded will admit that a long line of families engaged in eating, talking and singing, does not add to the dignity of a street. Incidentally, it appears that the new buildings on Herzl Street fronting the Technical Institution, are to be constructed from the same sand-stone as that building and will thus remain in keeping with a most beautiful piece of architecture. The Maccabi Hall, which was never meant to be other than temporary, will have to come down, but we are once again led to ask: does every new country pull down its buildings every few years ? Must a provisional structure be of concrete and left to deface the main thoroughfare with uncompleted rawness ?</p><p dir="auto">The Hadar Report goes on to speak of an enlarged shopping zone, essential to the increasing population, and I hear that a market has been planned, although the site has not been fixed. An effort is being made to keep the shopping district, as far as possible, round the Herzl St. area. That control is effective, for, in our street, there has existed only one shop since the days before restrictions were introduced; two other houses stand with gaping holes which await completion, and another proposed shop has had to become a carpentry. But beauty has not been sacrificed to comfort, for the housewife has only to walk to the next street, a few hundred yards away, to make her purchases. The price of water has not been reduced but part of the income from this source, apart from what is reinvested, is devoted to the purchase of communal plots and a parcel of 11,000 pics has already been purchased for a school and a park from the proceeds. Sewerage is still another problem that is being given due attention. Scavenging is being tackled and we are told that there is dissatisfaction with the Municipality's service in this respect. Over £P.3,880 was donated by the Committee to education and social service. Roads and pavements are being laid out, either directly by the suburb or as contractors for the Municipality (in the latter case at a loss it appears). Land has been obtained for the big new hospital which, however, has not yet been started. Haifaite</p><p dir="auto">DRAMA Local Products Revue The theatre has always been an excellent medium through which the temper and conditions of the times have been expressed. Like all other artistic forms it has been used not only to reproduce these conditions, but also for the purpose of shaping them. Propaganda plays, whether for war or peace, Bolshevism or pacifism, form a large portion of the dramatic output of the European and American stage to-day. These are high-flown phrases to introduce a trivial and popular play that has been crowding the auditorium of the Levant Fair at every presentation. However, the Matate* Company which gives this play has been a factor in the Palestinian drama for many years. Through the medium of revue it has been the politically satirical stage of this country. The revue has been the most popular form of entertainment in London, Paris and New York for a number of years. It is usually a quick running comment in the form of sketches, jokes and songs on the affairs of the day, with much display of the female, adorned and otherwise, to make the comment palatable to the tired business man. Palestinian business men are evidently not very tired and the female as such has been neglected. The rest of the ingredients have been present in the Matate performances. The present production has been written with the express purpose of boosting Palestine products and has been produced with even less subtlety than the Folies Bergeres or Mr. Ziegfeld used in glorifying the French or American girl. It is a sledgehammer effort to induce the public to buy goods manufactured in Palestine, and as such it may be as effective as any highly coloured poster. This blatant shouting of wares can hardly be dignified with the term propaganda and certainly has no dramatic effect. A great deal less belabouring of the point would surely have been more effective. If we can ignore the advertising aspect of Tozereth Ha-aretz, (local products) we have an amusing evening of light entertainment. The play presents a group of immigrants from almost every corner of the world, their trip to Palestine and their difficulties in getting adjusted to the new environment. From the poor Circassian who is not a doctor, and who has a great number of children who surprisingly enough want to eat, to the Palestinian girl who is returning after having been injected with European culture, they all come in for their share of good-natured lampooning. Each one speaks his particular brand of Hebrew with hilarious effect. The play was written by Emanuel Harussie and the music is by Verdina Shlonsky. Rather more attention than is usual with this company has been given to the dancing. The majority of the dances have been arranged by Miriam Hadanit, with solo dancing by Miss Hadanit and Naoma Lief. The dances have been designed to reflect the movement of the action in the scene and have succeeded in producing some interesting and attractive effects. The scene shifting is done in view of the audience, complete sets being noiselessly changed without any apparent difficulties. It is light, gay and amusing, and plays up to the feelings and emotions of the times, even to the final scene which ends on a highly romantic note in the wedding of the city to the land. This romanticism is very practical in as much as each promises to patronise the produce of the other. I.B.D.</p><p dir="auto">* Satiric theatre company.</p><p dir="auto">* Between Hadera and Zichron on the coast.</p>

<p dir="auto">THE WEEK IN COMMENT</p><p dir="auto">T\URING the present disturbances four Jewish women have been among the victims of the assassins' bullet. Terrible as must be the impression made upon all normal people by such cowardly and despicable crime, it can be said to the praise of the Jewish woman pioneer in Palestine that from the beginning of the Jewish emancipating movement, she has taken her place in everything, in danger and in joy, by the side of her male comrade. She has asked for no privileges of sex but only for equality of responsibility and opportunity. That ideal of a free and equal womanhood as part of a free and equal national status, she has followed faithfully unto death. Such is the deeper meaning of the tragedy of the loss of these women pioneers who by their sacrifice, needless and senseless though it be, have sealed the right of the Jewish woman to her full place in the nation's task. The era when "men must work and women must weep" has long been left behind by the Jewish national movement, one of the proudest features of which has been the recognition from its foundation of the absolute equality of men and women. The Change at Haifa For several months, the northern port withstood the propaganda of the Arab strikers, and functioned normally. In Haifa the public services at the harbour, the railways, and the petroleum works proceeded uninterrupted, and though a Municipal Commission succeeded the Municipal Council, local administration continued smoothly. Notwithstanding that particularly strong pressure was brought to bear on Haifa, where Jews and Arabs worked together and a Jewish-Arab labour organisation was founded, neither</p><p dir="auto">the emissaries of the Arab High Committee nor the acts of the terrorists caused any stoppage. It might have been thought that on the return of the District Commissioner of the North, the strengthened administration would make less likely the possibility of an undermining of Haifa's public activities. And yet if we are to believe the Arab press, the recent partial success of intimidation at Haifa is to be explained by the declaration of the District Commissioner that the general strike is legal provided that violence is avoided. It is difficult to believe that such statements were made but they have not been disavowed. Yet otherwise how is the change to be explained, and especially the weakness of the District Administration, precisely when energetic steps were required to nip in the bud the incitement and the intimidation. We cannot escape from the impression that toleration of the strike as a legal weapon (although an English judge pronounced in 1926 that a General Strike was illegal) has contributed to the encouragement of the strike agitators and to the indecision of those who should have suppressed the first indications of a threatened stoppage. The Moral If the Government has been able to report a considerable improvement in the labour situation at Haifa, the cause is to be found in the presence of the Jews, their participation in local public services and rapid mobilisation to save the situation. Hundreds of Arab strikers at the port were replaced by Jewish labourers, thus enabling it to be kept open. In place of the Arab porters, who left their jobs, at the Railway Station, forty Jews carried on,</p><p dir="auto">and the service did not suffer. When the Arab stokers gave up their work, a dozen Jewish stokers who had previously worked on the railways were recruited. It is a sad feature of the situation that the services of these Jewish workers who enabled the port of Haifa to function were accepted but grudgingly by the authorities. Great efforts were made to take on several hundreds of Hauranis, and it has been stated that when the Arab railway porters return, Jews who have stepped into the breach will be dismissed. In respect to the sanitary services, in which the Arab strikers resumed work for fear of losing their jobs, Jews were permitted to continue the work they had undertaken in place of the strikers, but only in the Jewish quarters. It should by now be apparent to the Government that the employment of Jews to an adequate extent in the public services is not merely an obligation to the Jewish population, but a vital necessity to the country as a whole if its public services are to be assured of stability and efficiency. The Jewish Elected Assembly The chief purpose of the Jewish Elected Assembly which held an extraordinary session this week was to express to the Government and to the Jews abroad the attitude of the local Jewish Community. This was done effectively in the manifesto which has been published, the contents of which will be placed before the High Commissioner by a delegation of the Assembly. The Assembly protested bitterly against the acts of the terrorists, and against the weakness of the Government which, unable to suppress the atrocities, has even caused them to be increased through weakly negotiating with the heads of the disturbances, thus creating an impression that the pressure of the terrorists is likely to cause a change in Government policy. The Assembly decided to issue a statement to the British people. As hitherto the Zionist Movement still considers a proper Palestine policy to be based principally upon parallel interests in this country of the British and the Jews. It is true that the attitude of the Government during these bloody months has considerably shaken Jewish confidence in the desire of the Government to follow such a policy. But this only obliges the Zionist Movement to renew its struggle on that same foundation which was laid twenty years ago. Turning within, the Assembly called upon the Jews here and abroad to increase their own efforts for the extension of the economic basis of the Jewish settlement by whole-heartedly supporting local Jewish products. Is the Terror to Continue ?</p><p dir="auto">The conference of Arab strike committees called for yesterday was cancelled by the Government on the plea that the excesses of the terrorists this week had rendered the atmosphere for such a meeting undesirable. It is quite possible that certain elements in the Arab camp have welcomed the postponement of a step which might have resulted in a repudiation of violence as a political weapon. But unfortunately, the voices of moderation are few indeed.</p><p dir="auto">The aggravated violence of the past week has been accompanied by increased intimidation within the Arab community itself, and it requires to-day great courage to urge peaceful and constitutional activity in place of terror. Those who have resolved upon the course of violence are evidently not satisfied with preventing any mediation by reasonable people in Palestine but are seeking to stir unrest also in the province of the Emir Abdullah, who has offered his intervention in the Palestine situation. So long as the extremists dominate, there can be no hope of the Arabs themselves putting an end to murderous and destructive methods. Even when the Arab National Committee of Jaffa was moved to express its horror of the latest outrage in that town, the murder of two Jewish nurses, it did not even suggest, or appeal for, the cessation of such violence. If the excuse be that the Arab authorities cannot influence the terrorists, it is one which will not easily be swallowed by the Palestine population, Arab or Jewish. An Additional Burden The Government has slowly recognised that, despite the additional military forces in the country, it is necessary to strengthen the police by the appointment of super-, numerary constables, especially in the Jewish settlements; which have been subjected to attacks for so many months.. The number of these extra police will apparently soon: reach 3,000, and there is no doubt whatsoever that their presence has forestalled the commission of more and worse crimes than those we have witnessed. The recruiting of these constables from among the Jewish community has git/en its members distinct satisfaction, for the opportunity^ to assist in defending themselves has been sought by the Jews since the peace was disturbed. But the condition accompanying this step, namely, that the Jews themselves must furnish the major cost of these additional policemen, is hard to understand. The strengthening of the forces bf security in the Jewish districts is not a private benefit, but a public service and a public obligation. The cr,st therefore should come from the same source as for any other branch of public services. The Jews, who are clearly those attacked, are suffering quite sufficiently both directly and indirectly, from the present disturbances; to impose upon them twothirds of the cost of public protection over and above their excessive contribution to the Treasury, is to penalise the peaceful element in favour of the lawless. Is there any precedent for such an imposition in any part of the British Empire, or, for that matter, in any foreign country ? Zionist in Conference</p><p dir="auto">The Jews of Palestine and abroad will await anxiously the outcome of the deliberations of the Zionist General Council, (the supreme Zionist organ in the interim between the sessions of the Zionist Congress), which meets next Wednesday at Zurich. The situation confronting the Council will require most weighty and serious discussion. It is expected that a united call will be issued giving a lead to the Jewish people in this dark: hour in the history</p><p dir="auto">of the rebuilding of Palestine. In this difficult period aggravated by obscure world conditions, the necessity to place the establishment of the National Home on such foundations as will withstand all shocks, is paramount. It is confidently hoped that the Council will rise to the height of its responsibilities. Review In our last issue we referred to the week then reviewed as the most wretched experienced. The past seven days have exceeded the previous week in tragedy. Four Jewish children between the ages of 5 and 8 were murdered in cold blood. Four young women, including two nurses of the Government Hospital in Jaffa, fell victims of murderous assaults. Seven men fell near Haifa, Zofith (by Kfar Saba) and Jaffa, thus bringing up the total Jewish deathroll to seventy. All these losses were a result of the violent increase of terror clearly intended to prevent the victory of "pacifist" tendencies among the Arabs themselves which had become more prominent during the previous week following upon the intervention of Emir Abdullah. An even more direct warning to Arab opponents of violence was the murder of the Mayor of Hebron, an opponent of the Mufti's party, who was killed by another Arab. Bloodshed being permitted and even blessed as the right way to serve the Arab cause, it is becoming increasingly difficult for the murderers to differentiate between their enemies, whether Jewish, British or Arab. Practically the whole country was involved in the outrages of the past week. It was in Safad that three children met their death together with their father in an attack which found the police altogether unprepared, although signs were abundant that violent assaults were to be expected. In Haifa, four young Jews paid the price of the breakdown of the most strenuous attempts made by the strike leaders to stultify the port and other public services. As if to avenge this failure, the fatal attack was made on the road leading to Carmel Forest. In Tel Aviv a bomb was buried on the beach on Saturday morning timed by electric wires to explode when large Jewish crowds were to be present. The Arab daily, Falastin later gloated that "had it exploded, it would have done wonders!" The wonders desired by Falastin were achieved by another bomb thrown from a train proceeding to Jaffa which killed a Jewish boy of eight, besides wounding some twenty persons. Later Jaffa exposed its degradation in the murder of two Jewish nurses on .the $taff of its local Government Hospital. The Jaffa railway station was closed and the curfew there extended for 20 hours per day. The stoppage of the train service between Tel Aviv and Jaffa followed the firing on a train on the boundary between the two towns when an Armenian passenger was killed and five Arabs wounded. One of the military guard was also slightly injured. About 15 Arabs were killed in various parts of the country, mainly in collision with troops and police. Attempts to attack convoys on the roads and to sabotage the railway communications were numerous, but did not succeed.</p><p dir="auto">Miscellany SACRED HOUSES AT JAFFA f HE Arab facility for pulling the leg of their British sympathisers and capitalising on a situation is remarkable. The sentimentality that has enveloped the sacred homes of Jaffa, recently destroyed by a wicked Government, would be amusing, if the implications behind this mawkish sympathy were not so obvious. The same British and Arab officials who wept as these rat and disease infested areas went up in huge clouds of dust, had never a word for the trees and grain and lives that have been destroyed. These houses that were demolished were part of the old city of Jaffa. But Jaffa is very much older than its old city. It was first mentioned in the Bible at the time of Ezra, and later Jonah embarked off the shore of Joppa for Tarshish. Its main historic significance seems to have been as a seaport for Jerusalem. At the time of the Maccabees, however, it was taken by Simon Maccabee and held over a period of about a hundred years. George Adam Smith in his Historical Geography of the Holy Land says of it "Joppa was therefore Jewish as no other town on the coast or maritime plain became, and so it continued until the campaign of Vespasian in 68 A.D., and it was violently Jewish." Whether violently Jewish or violently Arabic, Jaffa continued to be significant to Palestine mainly as the seaport of Jerusalem. It was on these stormy and rocky shores that Christian and Jewish pilgrims throughout the ages disembarked to traverse the holy way to Jerusalem. There are long periods when it seems to have fallen into obscurity, emerging only to be once more destroyed. At the time of the Crusades it changed hands several times and Saladin preferred to raze it to the ground rather than let it fall into Christian hands. From these ruins there gradually developed a typical Mediterranean port town with narrow tortured lanes serving as streets. The houses that lined these streets differed from the usual mud-brick houses only in the surprising thickness of the walls (in some places as much as four feet). One hundred years ago Jaffa had a population of four thousand. Since then the number has increased to much more than tenfold and has spread out into new and more attractive sections. Nothing, however, during the Turkish rule or after was done to improve the lot of the people who lived in the houses along these filthy lanes which wound their unsafe way down to the sea. The Government for some time had planned to demolish these dwellings in order to make room for wide streets which would relieve the congestion at the harbour. The Jaffa Port is now not merely a stopping place for Jerusalem pilgrims, but serves a thriving hinterland of hundreds of thousands of people. The fact that the order for the demolition in Jaffa came in evasive terms which brought forth censure from the Chief Justice, might have political significance. The fact that these narrow lanes and thick walls were a snipers' paradise probably had military significance. The fact,</p><p dir="auto">however, that the destruction of these dirty slums should be deplored both by British and Arabs has a great deal of social significance. In a normal country the erasure of such a blot would be more than welcomed. Every tremendous cloud of dust that rose with the explosion of thousands of pounds of dynamite should have been the occasion for satisfaction. Instead we still have a great deal of maudlin weeping over the destruction of these sacred homes and a huge mountain of debris remains to be carted away to make room for more sanitary if less sanctified dwellings. I. B. Davidowitz.</p>

<p dir="auto">HAIFA JEWS' BUDGET</p><p dir="auto">FROM TOWN AND COUNTRY</p><p dir="auto">QUIET RUSTICITY *** ARAB EXPORTERS PREFER NORTHERN PORT *** BRIDGING A WADI Haifa. DECEMBER came in like a lion, and between intermittent rain we have been having cold, crisp weather which makes sturdy Nordics from Eastern Europe and the Baltic close their windows and sit huddled over the kerosene stoves. Mount Hermon glistens white against a blue sky while the hills, the ships in the bay and the buildings in the plain stand with a clearness of outline which the summer did not vouchsafe us. Vendors of hot chestnuts throng Jaffa Road, shouting Kastaniya min Stamboul, and never have I known a city where the proportion of bad nuts to good is so large. The Municipality has been busy improvising drainage for the torrents which flow down from Carmel, bringing in their train stones and earth that litter the roadway to the mountain after very heavy rain. The town hums by day but in the evening, once the offices and shops close, it tends to become deserted with that eerie, hurrying solitude of Egypt at night ; and life moves to Hadar Hacarmel where Herzl Street, typically suburban in the morning, becomes a crowded thoroughfare after dark. The Hanuca menorot in Gan Benjamin (our park) and on the roof of the Technical College have barely gone out. Theatre, cinemas, lectures and concerts are in full swing. The blue lettering of the Palestine Symphony Orchestra advertisements are visible on every hoarding ; the name of Toscanini strikes the eye. The other week the circle of Jewish Youths from English-speaking countries gave a highly successful dance for officers stationed in Haifa. * * *</p><p dir="auto">The Committee of the Jewish Community, with some 50,000 souls under its jurisdiction, is still busy debating its new budget which will amount to some LP.30,000 and which, under the Communities Ordinance, must be ratified by the District Administration. The main item, as one would expect in a Jewish society, is education which accounts for 20% and is chiefly devoted to the upkeep of the Jewish National Council schools and public kindergartens within the area, while subsidies and donations are paid to private schools and cultural organisations. Physical training has its own special sub-heading. Next comes health, about 13%, being for the greater part the Community's share in the maintenance of the Hadassah Hospital, the balance consisting of special contributions towards the care of internal diseases, ringworm, insanity, and allowances for the Magen David Adom (First Aid) and Kupat Holim (Sick Fund). Public assistance entails a special staff and provision for immigrant aid, chronic invalids, the supply of matzot to the needy, and donations to the Jerusalem Blind Institute, Old Age Home, Orphanage, Children's Summer Home on Mount Carmel and playgrounds. Three other headings together absorb a further 20%: the Rabbinate (composed of Ashkenazi and Sephardi Rabbis), ritual cattle slaughter and other religious requirements. * * *</p><p dir="auto">The average tourist, while in Haifa, does not visit Neve Shaanan, the Jewish quarter on the spur known as the Red Carmel (although the name Carmel itself signifies red from the colour of its soil). Enjoying a dryness of air not to be found in the more popular parts of the mountain, Neve Shaanan has a wonderful view over the Mediterranean, north to the Syrian frontier and east to the gate of the Emek. Behind it stretches the plateau of Carmel, on the adjoining portion of which there is already land in Jewish possession ready for settlement. It gives the residents no pleasure to be told that there is a wonderful atmosphere of rural peace not often to be found in Palestine</p><p dir="auto">where each settlement is more or less a focus of bubblmg activity rather than a piece of settled country-side. This suburb has not drawn newcomers to the same extent as other districts, in spite of many attempts to give an impetus to its development, one most important reason being that up till the present access from the town lay only through Nazareth Road, that storm centre of every riot which occurs in Haifa. * * * For many years the project of a bridge across the valley, Wadi Rushmiya, between Neve Shaanan and Hadar Hacarmel, has been mooted and it appears that the dream may shortly become a reality. Contributions from the Committees of both these areas, from landlords along the line of the proposed bridge, and on the areas beyond Neve Shaanan which may be expected to gain from the new enterprise, and loans guaranteed by the Committee of Hadar Hacarmel—all will help to furnish the wherewithal for an undertaking which is expected to cost about LP.18,000, and to take nearly two years to complete. * * * The citrus season is in full swing and fruit is daily being brought to Haifa Port. Considerable damage was done by saboteurs to the railways during the Arab strike of last summer, but great efforts are being made to supply the maximum number of trucks. Fresh trucks have been ordered but it is feared that they will not arrive in time to cope with the demand of this winter, a demand made even greater by the number of Arab exporters who, dissatisfied with the methods of fruit inspection in force at Jaffa, are sending their oranges through Haifa. Haifaite.</p>

<p dir="auto">FROM TOWN AND COUNTRY</p><p dir="auto">Returning Home</p><p dir="auto">HAIFA OUT of the fog, frost and snow of Europe into the radiant air of the East. The first glimpse of Acre under the dawn-flushed hills, a slate sea silvering within its curve of sand, the gleam of metal drums, and piled white walls on the slope of Carmel: rich canvas spread for outer sight, that for months had 'strained inward through the glass of memory. Return, return to beauty, to the dazzle of sun and blue sky, olive-leaves shimmering, soft green of pines on terraced cliffs; to sanctuary of home and sacred soil. And also to the ugly shades of death and terror, violence of thought and act, the stalking form of murder. Sadly the tides of welcome flow back on a tale of havoc. Workers struck down in their fields, passengers sniped in car and bus, a milkman shot on his round, a child killed in the street; everywhere the sudden bomb and bullet, swifthurled on innocent heads. An incredible tale, as I stand once more on my balcony, and gaze across garden and waste to new roofs cut into the sweep of the sky and sea. The Arab shepherd moves leisurely in the rear of a herd of black cows, tinkling as they browse: Jewish builders clang their tools beneath the scaffolding of the nearest house: a neighbour's hens cluck, and delivery vans roll smoothly along the white roadway below my gates — the new kvish I have not seen before. It is all so peaceful, and normal, and progressive. The latter word will send a buzz into certain ears. The lady whom I met at tea yesterday is afflicted in this way. She has rambled the Carmel for many years, and was particularly fond of a field in which wild narcissi grew. "Last spring," she said, "I went as usual to pick flowers in my field. I found a house there!"— Only an English voice could express contempt so gently. It fell on me, for she added—"I believe it is your house!" I wilted, but not permanently. For I notice, without regret, that the progressive feature is marked throughout Haifa. Trade may fluctuate with the waves of crime, enterprise be checked, and building hampered. But the months of my absence have added considerably to the sum of Structure and improvement. The banks of Kingsway rise in dignified formation, a modern facade of flat cream brick, slotted with oblongs of green shutter. Beyond them the new railway-</p><p dir="auto">station presents a welcome front, with a wide rank for car and bus. When the rubbish heaps are cleared, it may prove as attractive as it is a convenient location. The Government Hospital at Bat Galim stands sheer, complete in architectural severity. Seen from the height of the old monastery, it throws up an arresting note, suggesting a newborn classic of the plain. The lower town has its island, green patches with bloom.</p><p dir="auto">The German Colony shows off its serried palms and peppers, olives, pines, and red-flowering shrubs, within low stone parapets and curving chains. Jaffa Road has at last a pavement, where so often I stumbled into potholes and ruined good leather shoes. More streets have names, and the mountain roads are appropriately signposted. Service has grown, or rather facilities have been extended —ready to be used when the paralysing hand is removd. For terror reigns. By day people crowd the busy streets, and appear not to heed the armed police who thread between. At sunset each corner and turning is deserted. The further reaches of crag, wood, and waste, on which the moon pours a silver flood, are uncannily still. Unofficial curfew robs nocturnal beauty of devotees, as it does the later business hours of custom. Not that all pleasure or relaxation is foregone. I arrived in time for the third concert of the Symphony Orchestra, and found the Armon Hall astonishingly full. If the scene lacked that animation and 6clat which belonged to the early performances of last season, it was only because magic names were missing. No less keen was the appreciation of fine music finely rendered. There can be only one Toscanini. But Mr. Steinberg is by no means a mere pedestrian conductor. He drew the powers of the orchestra to a consummate pitch in the interpretation of Mozart's Jupiter. In the Chopin concerto the soloist was supreme, though his rich, tender playing was enhanced by perfect accompaniment. The enthusiasm of the audience brought Jacob Gimpel back in continuous recall. Stravinsky's Petroushka was an interesting conclusion. I do not know how many of my neighbours enjoyed it, as I did, with the ballet vividly in mind. But even those who could not have been to Covent Garden seemed to relish the vigour and fantasy of the music. A happy concourse streamed out of the Armon, oblivious of armed guards at the doors. At the Teltsch Hotel a week-end gathering inaugurated a new guild of social fellowship. Songs and dances knit together a strange variety of Carmel residents. All languages could be heard, from Welsh to Turkish. The bridge of Hebrew does not quite span. And so the days and nights of care and tension are eased and lightened. If any adults give way to depression, they are shamed by the children. Among those who followed the murdered Haifa boy to his grave were two little schoolgirls. Their mother told me she had been invited by friends in Syria to bring her family away for a period of rest and relief. "Away," said the mother, "from danger." But the little girls scorned the invitation. "If it is dangerous here," they said, "all the more reason why we should stay. You can go if you like. We shall not leave Palestine." Clouds roll in from the horizon, heralding rain—"warm rain from Egypt," says the gardener, nodding sagaciously towards the West. "Not the hard cold rain from Syria." No matter whence it comes, rain is welcome, to freshen and recreate the earth. I look sadly at my roses, blighted by wind and ha'il. And at my whilom lawn, so green when I left —and now a stubble of brown. Serves you right," say, or hint, the knowing ones. They had laughed at me before. "What! You expect an English lawn in Palestine?" They were not impressed by the miracle of the emerald carpet that spread in a week of spring. And, as they foretold, it perished in the breath of summer. Now fresh seed has been sown—seed of a tougher, more localised kind. I still expect a lawn—a Palestinian lawn. LILY TOBIAS</p>
